Scope note: the attached assumption pools are mixed across candidates (the QO and NPB/KBO candidates carry coaching, rain-delay and draft assumptions). Each candidate below is judged only on its own IDEA text.

[Coaching hire] Recurrence is annual but small, at a few hires or retentions a year. Value per coach is asserted ("many players, multiple seasons") with no size supplied, so the stake is plausible but unquantified.

[Coaching hire] The data is lawful and public (staff announcements, Statcast), but "available at decision time" fails for assistant and minor-league roles. Tenure dates are inconsistently recorded, and a coach's actual role (who worked with whom) is not public.

[Coaching hire] Historical coach moves number perhaps in the low hundreds league-wide, but each coach touches few identifiable players. The outcome (player change) is observable, while the counterfactual is not.
[Coaching hire] Actionability is low-to-moderate. Hires are driven by fit, cost, manager preference and availability, and a noisy rating is unlikely to override them.

[Coaching hire] Clubs likely already evaluate coaches with private tracking data and player-development staff. Public Statcast gives only outcomes and pitch-level changes, not the coaching intervention.

[Coaching hire] It would look useful through regression to the mean (players are hired or moved after bad years), selection (teams acquire players they expect to improve), and playing-time, park and aging confounds. Overlapping coaches make credit unassignable, and ex-post storytelling about "coach X fixed him" will match any noisy result.

[Coaching hire] A falsifiable test is year-T-trained coach ratings predicting year T+1 player change at other clubs better than a prior-tenure reputation proxy, with out-of-time splits. A null result is the likeliest outcome and is itself informative.

[Non-tender] The decision recurs every year for the arbitration-eligible roster, with a late-November or early-December deadline. Value per case is the projected arbitration salary minus replacement cost, which is moderate and unquantified here.

[Non-tender] Projected arbitration salaries come from public comparables (MLBTR-style estimates), and non-tender lists are public after the deadline. The replacement market "that winter" is not known at the deadline, so the forecaster must predict who will be non-tendered league-wide, which is a hindsight trap.

[Non-tender] The history is roughly a decade or more of non-tender classes, with a modest number of notable cases per class. Outcomes (signing price, next-season production) are observable, though only for players who signed.

[Non-tender] Actionability is good, since the GM decides at a fixed date. The baseline (WAR per dollar against a threshold) is already a sound rule that clubs run, and the key inputs, the projection and its error, are the same ones public systems use.

[Non-tender] It would look useful if the backtest scores only players who were actually non-tendered and later succeeded (survivorship), or compares the model with a strawman threshold instead of the club's real rule. Small annual samples and the "played in MLB last year" lesson from the prior experiment suggest a simple rule captures most of the value.

[Qualifying offer] The decision recurs only if the club has eligible departing free agents, so expected annual value is discounted by that. The stake is the QO salary against a compensation pick, whose value depends on CBA terms not supplied.

[Qualifying offer] Public data at decision time includes age, WAR, injury history and the QO amount. Agent and market depth are weakly public, and acceptance behavior depends on private player preferences.

[Qualifying offer] Historical cases number perhaps a few dozen per year league-wide since 2012, which is far too few for a calibrated model with many features. Acceptance is rare and observable, but the counterfactual if a declined player had been accepted is not.

[Qualifying offer] Actionability is clear: a binary decision within days after the World Series. The baseline (offer when expected AAV clearly exceeds the QO) is close to the optimal structure, so only borderline cases are affected, which is a handful of players per decade for one club.

[Qualifying offer] It would look useful by overfitting dozens of cases and by describing rule changes as signal (QO amount, compensation rules and acceptance incentives shifted over time). The CBA transition may also change the QO regime, invalidating the training history.
[NPB/KBO posting] Events are few per year and the value per signing is potentially large. The Cubs are a bidder on only a subset, so expected yearly value is lumpy and dependent on who is posted.

[NPB/KBO posting] Public foreign-league stats are available, but the best pitch-tracking and bat-tracking data is often proprietary, so the public version of the model may be weaker than scouting. Posting windows are public only after the player is posted, and the contract price is set by competition, with a winner's-curse problem.

[NPB/KBO posting] The number of posted players with multi-season MLB outcomes is probably a few dozen to low hundreds over the posting era, split by hitter and pitcher, with differing league environments (ball and rule changes) over time. The outcome is observable but heterogeneous.
[NPB/KBO posting] Actionability is moderate, since the bid is the club's own decision, but the posted player's preferences, the posting fee rules and competing bids bound it.

[NPB/KBO posting] Sophisticated clubs already run translation models and employ Asia-based scouts, and public sources (Fangraphs-style ZiPS translations) provide baselines. It would look useful when a few famous successes or busts are fitted post hoc, when the sample is dominated by stars, or when the test compares it with a naive ratio rather than with published translations.

[Postseason roster] The decision recurs only when the club qualifies, about 1 to 4 roster sets in a qualifying year. The stake is per-series win probability, and the marginal roster slots (25th and 26th men) probably move it by a small amount, which is unquantified.

[Postseason roster] Opponent, rotation and public splits are largely public before a series, but health and availability are not fully public at the deadline, and the managers' actual usage plan is private.

[Postseason roster] The history is a few dozen series per year league-wide, and rosters are not randomly assigned, so the outcome (series result) is observable but swamped by game-level noise. An effect of a percentage point cannot be detected from that history.
[Postseason roster] Actionability is decent for the final roster spots, but managers concentrate usage on the top relievers and starters regardless, and health often forces the choice.

[Postseason roster] Contenders likely run private simulations. It would look useful through simulated gains that cannot be falsified, by scoring on the winners' rosters, or by crediting a roster with a series result that is mostly luck.

[Arbitration filing] The decision recurs every January across the arbitration-eligible roster, and awards compound into later raises. The stake is the gap between the filing midpoints, which is typically small per player, so the total is meaningful but bounded.

[Arbitration filing] Filing figures and hearing results are public after the exchange. The panels' reasoning and settlements are not fully recorded, and the CBA's arbitration rules may change, which would shift the process.

[Arbitration filing] Hearings number only a handful per year league-wide (possibly single digits to low teens), so over a decade there might be on the order of 100, with a heavy dependence on a few decision panels. The outcome is observable (the club or the player wins), but only for cases that went to a hearing, which is a selected sample.

[Arbitration filing] Actionability is high on a short timeline, but many clubs follow a file-and-trial policy that they treat as strategic rather than outcome-driven, and the settlement option constrains the filing number.

[Arbitration filing] Clubs and outside firms already hold this knowledge, and the standard comparables rules make the midpoint baseline hard to beat. It would look useful through overfitting a small hearing set, ignoring selection into hearings, or reporting accuracy on hearing wins that the midpoint already predicts.

Blind spot: the set is dominated by small-N annual decisions. The prior experiment's lesson, that a simple baseline captures most value, applies to most of them, so each needs a stated minimum detectable effect before building anything.

Blind spot: a retrospective test can mislead through look-ahead on projections and through market-clearing prices that already contain the information. No candidate states a "decision-time snapshot" archive requirement, and archived projections and arbitration estimates may not exist.
Blind spot: the candidates share a CBA-expiry dependency (arbitration, QO, service time, draft rules), so the history may stop being predictive after the next agreement.
Blind spot: the value at stake is unquantified for all six candidates, and no ranking by expected dollars or wins per year is possible with the supplied evidence.
Blind spot: the Cubs' internal tools are unknown, so "edge over the club's baseline" cannot be measured. The only honest comparator is a published public baseline.

Sharpened replacement: run a pre-registered "baseline-versus-model" harness in which, for each candidate, the decision-time snapshot, the club's simple rule, a minimum detectable effect and the number of available historical cases are fixed before any model fitting. Build software only for decisions that pass (likely the non-tender and tender workflow, using frozen public projections and arbitration estimates as inputs), and treat coaching attribution as a research test whose null result would be informative.

Coaching hire evaluation (sharpened) - build a public coach-movement ledger, but use it first as a falsification study across all 30 clubs to test whether coach-attributed player change persists year over year, and only then as a hiring screen, with a pre-registered kill criterion.
Coaching hires recur yearly, but a club fills only a handful of major-league and upper-minors slots, so the per-club decision count is small even if league-wide history is larger.
Public staff announcements and media guides may be incomplete or misdated for assistant and minor-league roles, so coach-to-player linkage may be wrong.

Coach effects are confounded by roster turnover, playing time, selection of players a club expects to improve, organizational infrastructure, and regression to the mean, so unidentifiable effects are a live possibility.

Most coaches touch few movers, so intervals may be too wide to change a hiring decision; the test is whether year-T ratings predict year T+1 better than a reputation proxy such as prior big-league tenure.
The outcome is observable (player metrics) but the counterfactual is not, so the test is predictive, not causal.

Non-tender decisions (sharpened) - rather than a forecaster of the whole replacement market, backtest only the marginal tender/non-tender call for borderline players, using projected arbitration salary (public estimates available before the deadline) against what comparable non-tendered players actually signed for and produced afterward.
The decision recurs every late November and the number of borderline players per club is small, so value per year is likely modest and unquantified here.

Projected arbitration salaries, non-tender lists and signings are public, but the replacement market is only partly known at the deadline since non-tendered players are revealed at the deadline itself; using the later list is hindsight.

Historical non-tender cases number in the dozens per year league-wide, so a retrospective test is feasible, and next-season output is observable, though survivorship bias (only those who signed have outcomes) and injury noise distort it.

Clubs likely already apply a WAR-per-dollar threshold and private projections, so a public model may merely reproduce the baseline; it would look useful if backtested using the full list known after the deadline.

The pool is near the low-attention minor-league free-agent pool that a prior experiment found yielded under one contributor per club per year, so a ceiling of similar size is plausible.

Qualifying offers (sharpened) - treat as a small pooled-league calibration exercise, valuing the offer decision with an explicit acceptance probability and the draft-pick value under current rules, rather than a Cubs-specific model.
The decision recurs only when the club has an eligible departing free agent, so expected annual value is discounted by how many such players exist.
Public QO history has only a handful of cases per year and acceptance has been rare, so a model may not beat a simple "offer if market AAV clearly exceeds the QO" rule.
Pick compensation value depends on revenue-sharing and tax status and on current CBA terms, which must be verified; a CBA transition could change or end the system.
Agent and player preferences, which are private, dominate acceptance, and the counterfactual of the player being offered or not is unobservable for non-offered players.
Backtests would look good if the market AAV used was the post-signing actual value rather than a forecast at decision time.

NPB/KBO posting bids (sharpened) - build a translation model with wide uncertainty intervals and use it mainly to set a walk-away price that guards against the winner's curse, not to find bargains.
Few events per year, so value is large per signing but sparse; the Cubs may face none in a given year.
The number of posted players with MLB outcomes is small, perhaps too small to beat simple ratios, and outcomes are heavily influenced by injury and adjustment.
Pitch-tracking data for NPB and KBO may not be fully public; posting rules and fee structures must be verified for the current window, and the player must choose a club, which limits actionability.
Club scouts see these players in person and international departments are already experienced; public stats tools exist, so edge may be near zero.
Looks useful if a model is fit with league-environment changes known only after the fact or if a few star successes drive calibration.

Postseason roster construction (sharpened) - evaluate only the last two roster slots and the pitcher-count choice, using league-wide public postseason rosters and a simulation of marginal slot value, and report the win-probability value first; build further only if it exceeds a pre-set threshold.
The decision recurs at most a few times a year and only when the club qualifies; the Cubs' 2026 season ended in the Wild Card Series, so there is no decision this fall.
The value of a marginal slot is probably well under one percentage point of series win probability, and managers concentrate use on a few players.
Public rosters, box scores and transactions are available, but injury status and the opponent's lineup choices at decision time are only partly public; reconstructing alternatives risks hindsight.

The retrospective test has very few series per club, and the actual outcome of a single short series is mostly noise, so a recommended roster cannot be shown better; only a simulation can, and that embeds the model's own assumptions.
Contending clubs likely already run such simulations privately.

Arbitration filing (sharpened) - a settle-versus-hearing expected-value calculator that only needs public filing figures and results, applied to the few cases where the gap between filed numbers is large.

The decision recurs every January across all arbitration-eligible players, but hearings are rare, perhaps a handful per year league-wide, so the hearing outcome sample is small and the club's own cases fewer still.
Filing figures and hearing results are public, but panel reasoning is not, and the CBA's arbitration rules may change in a new agreement.
Midpoint settlement is a strong baseline; a model looks useful if it fits past hearings after choosing features that panels are known to reward, which is overfitting to a small sample.
Clubs have specialized staff and outside experience, and teams that file and go to trial may suffer relationship costs with players that no public data can measure.

BLIND SPOT - every candidate relies on labels that are confounded or only partly observable, and several rely on later-known information such as the full non-tender list, final market AAV or season outcomes, which creates hindsight leakage.
BLIND SPOT - none addresses the CBA, which may expire around this offseason (unverified) and could change QO, arbitration, and service rules, invalidating history.

Every critique below is judgment from general baseball-operations structure. None is verified, and no figure is quoted because none was supplied.
The attached assumptions are pooled across many ideas, and many (rain delays, stolen bases, draft pools, ticketing) are irrelevant to these six. Only those matching each IDEA text are used.
[1 Coaching hire] The decision recurs only a few times a year, and each hire is a single, unrepeatable choice. The value at stake is unquantified, and the ledger's sign is unknown.
[1] Public staff data is not point-in-time clean. Titles, assistant and minor-league roles and start dates in press releases and media guides are incomplete and revised after the fact.

[1] Few players move organizations alongside a given coach. Movers are selected (acquired because the club expects improvement) and coach credit is shared among several staff. Playing time, health and the player's own regression to the mean are further confounders.

[1] A retrospective test is possible if ratings built through year T predict player change under the same coach in T+1 better than a tenure-and-reputation proxy. The number of coaches with enough movers may be too small for intervals narrow enough to change a hire.
[1] Outcome observability is weak because the counterfactual is missing. Clubs with private tracking and biomechanics data probably evaluate coaches better than any public panel can.

[1] It would look useful by ranking coaches whose past-year gains are mostly regression to the mean. The ranking would look reasonable with no persistence, so year-over-year persistence is the key falsification test.

[2 Non-tender] This recurs annually with a hard early-December deadline (unverified; the CBA may change it). The value at stake is each eligible player's projected arbitration salary minus replacement cost, which is real but unquantified.

[2] Salary projections are public-ish and available at decision time. The replacement market (who will be non-tendered league-wide, and at what price) is not known when the Cubs decide, so the forecaster must predict other clubs' choices.

[2] A backtest has many player-years, but price and next-season output are observed only for players who signed. Players who retired, went abroad or signed minor-league deals create survivorship bias.

[2] The baseline (tender if WAR per dollar beats a threshold) is the same quantity the forecaster uses, so gains may be only a threshold re-tune. The prior finding that a simple rule captures most of the value in the low-attention pool suggests a ceiling here too.

[2] It would look useful from post-hoc selection of bargain non-tendered players, where single-season WAR noise is large and winners are remembered. Sophisticated clubs already carry internal projection and arbitration models.

[3 Qualifying offer] The decision is annual but applies only to the Cubs' own pending free agents who meet eligibility rules. The Cubs' eligible list is unknown, so expected value may be near zero in many years.

[3] The QO amount, acceptances and signings are public, but the number of cases per year is small. The accepted and declined classes are lopsided, so calibration is weak and one executive's judgment may match it.

[3] The idea's baseline ("offer when market AAV clearly exceeds the QO") already needs a market AAV estimate. The model replaces that estimate, so the claimed edge reduces to forecast accuracy on a handful of players.

[3] The compensation-pick value depends on CBA terms that may change at expiration (unverified). Counterfactual value cannot be observed, and acceptance is driven by player preference, health and agent strategy that public signals miss.
[3] It would look useful through rare, memorable accepted-QO cases and high accuracy on obvious calls such as a star who is declined.
[4 NPB/KBO posting] This is a handful of events per year across the league, and the Cubs only matter when they pursue a given player. Per-signing value is plausibly large but unquantified.
[4] The posting window is largely public. Ownership of NPB pitch-tracking and detailed batted-ball data is limited, and what is public may lag decision time.

[4] Previously posted players with MLB outcomes are few, so the translation model has high variance and heterogeneous eras and league environments. Outcomes are observable but censored, because players who were not signed leave no MLB data.

[4] The winner's curse means a more accurate public model still does not give an edge unless the Cubs bid below the consensus. Clubs with international scouting, video and private data are likely ahead, and the idea overlaps minor-league translation work.
[4] It would look useful by fitting the few posted stars in hindsight, with overfit coefficients and nothing out of sample.

[5 Postseason roster] The decision recurs only in years the Cubs qualify, one to four times a year by the candidate's own text. Expected annual value is discounted by qualification probability (unknown).
[5] Rosters, opposing starters and platoon splits are public at the decision time. Injury status at the roster deadline may be incompletely public.

[5] Pooled league-wide postseason rosters give a modest number of series, but each series outcome is dominated by noise. A series-win-probability difference from the 25th and 26th roster spots may be too small to detect with any realistic sample.
[5] Alternatives are not observed, so the backtest is a simulation scored by its own model and can embed the biases it tests. Clubs likely already run internal series simulators.
[5] It would look useful by retrofitting a few memorable pinch-runner or reliever moments in a winning run, which is outcome bias.

[6 Arbitration filing] This recurs every January across the arbitration-eligible roster, and awards compound into later raises, so it is among the more regular decisions. The value is capped by the gap between the two filed numbers, since the panel picks one.

[6] Filed numbers, results and the comparable-player rules are largely public. The exact arguments and the panel's reasoning are not, and hearings are rare because most cases settle. Settlements are not hearing outcomes, so the training labels come from a selected subset.

[6] The count of historical hearings may be too small and shifts with CBA rule changes (expiration date and new rules unverified). Whether to settle or go to hearing is a strategic choice also tied to club policy and player relations, not just EV.

[6] The baseline (midpoint settlement) is a hearing-free outcome, so the EV comparison needs an assumed hearing probability and a model of player willingness. Specialized staff and outside counsel probably already hold this knowledge.

[6] It would look useful through a predictor tuned to hearing outcomes in which the filing midpoint alone already predicts the winner, and through ignoring that club-won and player-won cases are selected by who chose to go to hearing.
[Blind spot] Dollar and win value at stake is unquantified for all six. Rank the candidates by value times decision count times the maximum plausible edge before building anything.

[Blind spot] Sample size is the shared weakness (QO, posting, postseason, hearings, coach movers). Pooling league-wide raises n but strips Cubs-specific context, and no tool can beat a simple baseline with only a few dozen noisy labels.

[Blind spot] Many of these decisions are driven by counterparties (agents, player preference, rival bidders, the league). A club-side prediction model does not control the outcome, and the rules may change at the CBA expiration (unverified).
[Blind spot] Dated snapshots are a precondition. Any backtest must freeze the data as of the decision day (projections, injury status, staff titles), or hindsight leaks into every candidate.

[Blind spot] Testing many candidates and many specifications without a pre-registered baseline comparison produces false positives. Any claimed edge needs out-of-sample results against the simple rule.

[Blind spot] Non-tender, QO, arbitration and posting all draw on one payroll and 40-man budget, so evaluating them separately misses interactions. Private Cubs practice is unknown, and public-data parity with sophisticated clubs is plausible for every candidate.

Build a single pre-registered, dated-snapshot backtest harness for the offseason decisions (non-tender, QO, arbitration, posting). It would freeze public inputs as of each decision date, score each simple club baseline against a candidate model out of sample, and report n and interval width, so any candidate whose interval includes zero edge is dropped before software is built.

Replace the coaching-ledger build with a persistence-first test: check on public data whether apparent coach effects in year T repeat in T+1 for coaches who moved clubs. Proceed to a hiring tool only if they persist beyond regression to the mean, and treat a null result as the useful output.

Sharpen arbitration to settle-versus-hearing selection: estimate, from public filed-number gaps and past outcomes, the filing-gap threshold above which hearings favor the club. State the result as a decision table with explicit uncertainty rather than a point predictor.

All evidence is UNVERIFIED and the facts map is empty, so every judgment below is a falsifiable critique drawn from general baseball knowledge, not a supported finding. CITE lines are omitted because no source supports any specific claim.
Coaching-hire evaluation (1) The decision recurs every offseason but only a few hires per year, and the value per coach is unknown. UNKNOWN: detectable_coach_effect_size
Coaching (2) Staff announcements are public, but assistant and minor-league tenure is patchy and inconsistently dated, so linking coaches to players at decision time may fail.

Coaching (3) Coach moves between organizations are few, and most coaches touch few players, so a retrospective test has wide intervals. Outcomes are observable only as player stat changes, not as coach causation.

Coaching (4,5) Hiring is driven by relationships, scheme fit and player buy-in that a panel cannot see. Rival clubs probably run private attribution with proprietary biomechanics and tracking data, so a public-data tool is likely behind.

Coaching (6) It will look useful through regression to the mean, since players hired-for-after-a-bad-year improve anyway. Selection (teams acquire players they expect to improve), playing time, injuries and org infrastructure confound it. Post-hoc coach rankings that do not persist year over year would look good in-sample and fail out of sample.

Non-tender (2) Service time, projected arbitration salaries (public estimates exist) and the non-tender list are public, but the replacement pool is revealed only after the deadline. A forecast of who will be available must be made without hindsight, and that is the hard part.

Non-tender (3) Roughly two decades of non-tender classes exist, but the CBA has changed salary and service rules, so older cases may not be comparable. Next-season output of non-tendered players is observable, but the output of the counterfactual tendered player is not, and survivorship in who signs where biases the comparison.

Non-tender (4,5) It is actionable, since the club decides by the deadline. Clubs already use WAR-per-dollar thresholds, and public arbitration projection tools exist, so the marginal edge is likely small.

Non-tender (6) A backtest looks good when it credits signed non-tendered players' production without netting out the many who flopped or were never signed, or when it uses the final arbitration salary instead of the projection known in November.

Qualifying offers (1) The Cubs face the decision only for their own eligible free agents, which may be zero to a few per year. The stake is a one-year QO salary against a draft-pick change, so the value is moderate and lumpy. UNKNOWN: cubs_qo_eligible_players_2026
Qualifying offers (2) Performance, age and the QO amount are public. Acceptance depends on private player preferences and agent strategy.

Qualifying offers (3) The number of historical QOs is a few dozen per year at most, with an early period of nearly zero acceptances and a later period with some, so the pooled model is small and non-stationary. Acceptance is observable, but the counterfactual of not offering is not. UNKNOWN: historical_qo_acceptance_count_by_year

Qualifying offers (4,5) It is actionable in a short window after the World Series. Clubs reason about this with simple market-versus-QO logic, and a sharper model probably adds little over an experienced executive.

Qualifying offers (6) A high AUC in-sample may come from a few features (large AAV expectation means decline) that the baseline already uses. Rule changes to compensation across CBAs also confound the pooled history.

NPB/KBO (3) The number of posted players with several MLB seasons is small, probably tens, split across hitters and pitchers and across ball and rule eras. A model with many parameters will overfit. Outcomes are observable but heterogeneous by role and injury. UNKNOWN: count_of_posted_players_with_mlb_outcomes

NPB/KBO (4,5) Bids are actionable only in a short, rule-bound window and posting fees and caps depend on current agreements. Clubs with international scouts and data staff already model translation, and the price is set by multi-club competition, so the winner's curse may erase any accuracy edge.
NPB/KBO (6) It looks useful through survivorship (only successes recalled), a few outlier stars driving fit, and comparing to the weakest ratio baseline instead of scouting-informed pricing.

Postseason roster construction (1) It recurs only when the club qualifies, 1 to 4 times a year, so expected value is discounted by playoff probability. A marginal win may be worth more in October, but the number of slots that actually change outcomes is small. UNKNOWN: measured_win_probability_value_of_marginal_postseason_slot

Postseason (2) Rosters, platoon and pitch-type splits are public, but injury status at the roster deadline is often incomplete or vague, which limits reconstruction of the true option set. UNKNOWN: public_injury_status_completeness_at_roster_deadline

Postseason (3) Postseason rosters from many series exist league-wide, but the per-series sample is tiny and series outcomes are very noisy. A test would need to score recommendations by simulated expected win probability, and the simulation embeds the same assumptions it tests, so it is not an observed-outcome validation.
Postseason (4,5) It is actionable and contenders already do this internally with staff judgment, so a public tool likely only matches.

Postseason (6) It looks useful through hindsight-chosen anecdotes (a pinch runner who scored), unmeasurable gains of well under a percentage point of series win probability, and ignoring that managers concentrate innings on top pitchers whatever the 26th slot is. Note the candidate text supplied for this item lists only the decision, and the problem is narrower than its attached assumptions suggest.

Arbitration filing (1) The Cubs file for each arbitration-eligible player every winter, which is several per year, with award differences per player in the range between filing numbers. Most cases settle, and hearings are rare for any one club.

Arbitration (2) Hearing outcomes and filing figures are publicly reported, but the panel's reasoning is confidential, and settlement terms are inconsistently recorded. Comparable-player selection rules are set by the CBA, which may change after this offseason. UNKNOWN: post_2026_cba_arbitration_rules
